title: Leg Pain or Heaviness When Walking: Is It Spinal Stenosis (Narrow Spinal Canal)?
metaDescription: Leg pain, heaviness or weakness when walking that eases on sitting may be spinal stenosis. Learn the signs, treatment options and warning symptoms.
intro: Leg pain, heaviness or weakness that comes on with walking or standing, and eases when you sit or lean forward, can be a sign of spinal stenosis. This means the space around the spinal nerves has become narrow. Many people are helped by medicines and exercise. Surgery is only one option, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: What is spinal stenosis?
sections.body: Spinal stenosis happens when the space around the spinal cord and spinal nerves gets smaller. The narrowing can press on the nerves and cause leg pain, numbness or weakness. According to OrthoInfo, arthritis is the most common cause. With age, the discs between the bones lose water and shrink, the joints can wear and form bone spurs, and the ligaments can thicken. Some people are born with a narrower canal, but this is less common.

sections.heading: What does it feel like?
sections.body: Pain often spreads from the buttock down the leg and may feel like an ache or burning. You may also notice numbness, tingling or weakness, and some people feel unsteady when walking. Standing up straight or walking usually makes symptoms worse. Sitting or leaning forward usually helps, so many people find they must stop and rest after a short distance. Sometimes the foot catches or slaps the ground while walking.

sections.heading: Why does leaning forward help?
sections.body: Leaning forward can increase the space available for the nerves, as OrthoInfo explains. Harvard Health makes the same point: symptoms often worsen when the spine is straight and ease when you bend forward. This pattern is a useful clue for your doctor, together with an examination.

sections.heading: Can it be treated without surgery?
sections.body: Often, yes. OrthoInfo says non-surgical treatment does not reverse the narrowing, but many people report that it helps relieve symptoms. Our usual approach is medicines first for pain, such as anti-inflammatory tablets used for the shortest time needed. Once pain eases, we advise stretching and core strengthening exercises, and walking aids if balance is a problem. Care is tailored to your symptoms, your other health conditions and how far you wish to walk.

sections.heading: Do injections help?
sections.body: Epidural steroid injections can reduce pain and numbness for some people, but OrthoInfo says they do not help weakness and advises no more than three a year. Harvard Health calls steroid injections temporary relief, not a long-term solution. NICE guidance for low back pain and sciatica says not to use epidural injections for leg symptoms from central canal narrowing. Because of this mixed picture, we offer injections only to selected patients, and only for pain relief.

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body: Surgery is generally considered when pain or weakness, including difficulty walking, seriously affects quality of life despite other treatment. The usual operation, called laminectomy (decompression), removes bone, bone spurs and ligaments pressing on the nerves. Fusion is added when the spine is unstable. Risks include bleeding, infection, nerve injury and not relieving symptoms. We explain the options and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When is leg pain an emergency?
sections.body: Rarely, nerve compression becomes a medical emergency called cauda equina syndrome. Go to an emergency department at once if you have numbness around the genitals or anus, loss of bladder or bowel control, or leg weakness that is getting worse quickly. Also seek prompt help for fever, a recent injury, unexplained weight loss, or pain that is worse at night.

faqs.q: Is leg pain on walking always spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Leg pain has many possible causes, so an examination is needed. The pattern of relief on sitting or leaning forward is a helpful clue.

faqs.q: Does a narrow spinal canal get worse over time?
faqs.a: Wear and tear in the spine is common with age. Not everyone with such changes has symptoms, and treatment depends on how much trouble you have.

faqs.q: Is walking harmful if I have spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: Walking may bring on symptoms, and sitting or leaning forward usually helps. Ask for exercise advice suited to you.
It does not reverse the narrowing. Stretching and strengthening can still help you manage symptoms and keep moving.

faqs.q: Do I always need surgery for spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: No. Surgery is generally considered only when symptoms seriously affect your life or walking despite other treatment, and the choice is yours.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after decompression surgery?
faqs.a: OrthoInfo says most people can return to a desk job within a few days to a few weeks. Full activity usually resumes in 2 to 3 months, and fusion adds time.
